services-concrete-lifting.h1: Concrete Lifting Services in Omaha, NE
services-concrete-lifting.hero_subhead: Concrete lifting raises sunken slabs back to (or near) their original position without full replacement. See how it works and get matched with local Omaha contractors.

body_sections.heading: Overview
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown:
"Concrete lifting" is the umbrella term for methods that raise a settled or sunken concrete slab back into place, instead of tearing it out and pouring new concrete. The two most common approaches used by contractors in the Omaha area are mudjacking (injecting a cement-based slurry) and polyjacking (injecting expanding polyurethane foam). Both aim to fill voids under the slab and lift it back to grade.

Omaha Concrete Lift is an independent referral service. We are not a contractor and do not perform concrete leveling work ourselves. Learn how our matching service works or read our full referral disclosure.

body_sections.heading: How This Method Generally Works
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: In general, a contractor drills small holes (often 5/8" to 1.5" depending on method and equipment) through the slab, pumps material underneath to fill voids and lift the slab, then patches the holes. The exact process, hole size, material, and cure time varies by contractor and by the specific method used — always confirm details with the contractor who quotes your project.

body_sections.heading: Signs You May Need This Service
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown:
• One or more corners or edges of a slab sit lower than the rest
  • Visible gaps or cracks where two slab sections meet
  • Water pooling in areas that used to drain properly
  • A slab that has become a trip hazard
  • Doors or gates that no longer clear a nearby slab

body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: Explore specific applications: driveways, sidewalks, patios, and garage floors.

services-mudjacking.hero_subhead: Mudjacking is a long-standing method for raising sunken concrete using a cement-based slurry. Get matched with local Omaha contractors who offer it.

body_sections.heading: Overview
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown:
Mudjacking (sometimes called slab jacking) is one of the oldest and most widely used concrete lifting methods. A contractor pumps a mixture typically made of soil, sand, cement, and water beneath a settled slab to fill voids and raise it back toward its original position.

Omaha Concrete Lift is an independent referral service. We are not a contractor and do not perform concrete leveling work ourselves. Learn how our matching service works or read our full referral disclosure.

body_sections.heading: How This Method Generally Works
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: Holes are drilled into the slab (commonly around 1.5 to 2 inches, though this varies by contractor), the slurry mix is pumped underneath under pressure, and the slab is monitored as it lifts. Holes are then patched. Because the mix is heavier than foam alternatives, some contractors prefer it for certain soil types or larger slabs — but material choice, pricing, and technique vary by company, so ask your matched contractor about their specific process.

body_sections.heading: Signs You May Need This Service
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown:
• Large driveway or patio slabs with significant settling
  • Budget-conscious projects where a heavier, traditional fill material is preferred
  • Situations where a contractor's experience and local soil knowledge favor a cement-based approach

services-polyjacking.h1: Polyjacking (Polyurethane Foam Concrete Lifting) in Omaha, NE
services-polyjacking.hero_subhead: Polyjacking uses expanding polyurethane foam to lift sunken concrete. Get matched with local Omaha contractors offering this method.

body_sections.heading: Overview
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown:
Polyjacking — also called polyurethane foam injection or foam jacking — uses a lightweight, expanding two-part foam instead of traditional slurry. The foam is injected beneath the slab, where it expands to fill voids and lift the concrete.

Omaha Concrete Lift is an independent referral service. We are not a contractor and do not perform concrete leveling work ourselves. Learn how our matching service works or read our full referral disclosure.

body_sections.heading: How This Method Generally Works
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: Contractors typically drill smaller holes than mudjacking requires (often around 5/8 inch, though this varies), inject the foam, and the slab can often be walked on again relatively quickly after treatment — actual cure and return-to-use times vary by contractor, product, and project size. The foam is generally lighter and more water-resistant than cement slurry, which some contractors point to as an advantage for certain soil or drainage conditions.

body_sections.heading: Signs You May Need This Service
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown:
• Homeowners who want a less invasive repair with smaller holes
  • Areas with drainage or moisture concerns where a water-resistant fill material may be preferred
  • Projects where minimizing weight added to the sub-base matters

faq.hero_subhead: General, honest answers to common questions about concrete leveling, mudjacking, and polyjacking. For project-specific numbers, a local contractor quote is always the most accurate source.

body_sections.heading: Why does concrete sink or settle in the first place?
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: Concrete slabs themselves don't usually deteriorate — the soil underneath them does. Common causes include soil compaction over time, erosion from water runoff, poor original sub-base preparation, freeze-thaw cycles, and organic material that decomposes under the slab and leaves a void. Once support underneath the slab is lost, gravity and traffic load cause it to settle unevenly.

body_sections.heading: What's the difference between mudjacking and polyjacking?
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: Mudjacking uses a cement-based slurry pumped beneath the slab to fill voids and lift it, typically through larger drilled holes. Polyjacking uses an expanding polyurethane foam injected through smaller holes. Foam is generally lighter and more water-resistant, while slurry is a heavier, longer-established material. Cost, hole size, cure time, and suitability for your specific project varies by contractor and by soil/site conditions — a local contractor can advise which fits your project best.

body_sections.heading: How much does concrete leveling cost?
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: Cost varies by contractor, region, slab size, method (mudjacking vs. polyjacking), and how much lifting is needed. There isn't a single reliable number we can quote here — pricing varies by contractor and project, which is exactly why getting a few quotes from local pros is useful.

body_sections.heading: How long does a concrete leveling job typically take?
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: Many residential leveling jobs (a driveway panel, a sidewalk slab, a small patio) can be completed in a matter of hours to a single day, but this varies by contractor, method, equipment, and the size/scope of the project. A contractor can give you a project-specific estimate after assessing the site.

body_sections.heading: Is concrete leveling a permanent fix?
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: Concrete leveling addresses the existing void and settling at the time of the repair, but if the underlying cause (drainage, soil erosion, an ongoing leak, etc.) isn't resolved, settling can recur over time. Ask your contractor what, if anything, they recommend to address the root cause, and what warranty (if any) they offer — warranty terms vary by contractor.

body_sections.heading: Can concrete leveling fix a cracked slab, or do I need full replacement?
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: Leveling raises a slab back toward its original position; it doesn't repair existing cracks, though many contractors can seal or patch cracks as part of the job. Whether leveling makes sense versus full replacement depends on the extent of cracking, slab age, and condition — this varies by contractor and by inspection findings.

body_sections.heading: Is concrete leveling less expensive than replacing the slab?
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: In many cases, leveling costs less than full slab removal and replacement, since it reuses the existing concrete rather than requiring demolition, disposal, forming, and a new pour. That said, actual cost comparisons vary by contractor, project scope, and site conditions — a quote from a local pro is the most reliable way to compare.

body_sections.heading: Will concrete leveling affect my landscaping or driveway access?
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: Most leveling methods involve small drilled holes and don't require large-scale excavation, so impact on landscaping is typically minimal compared to full replacement. Access needs (e.g., temporarily blocking a driveway) vary by contractor and project — ask about this when you get your quote.

body_sections.heading: Do I need to be home when the contractor comes out?
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: This depends on the contractor's process and whether it's an initial assessment or the actual leveling work. Many contractors can provide an initial estimate without you being present, but policies vary — the contractor who contacts you can confirm what's needed.

body_sections.heading: How do I verify a contractor is licensed and insured?
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown: Always ask any contractor directly for proof of their business license, insurance, and any relevant certifications before hiring them, and verify this information independently if possible (for example, through Nebraska or Iowa state licensing resources, if applicable in your area). Omaha Concrete Lift does not verify, certify, or guarantee the licensing or insurance status of contractors in its network — see our referral disclosure.

body_sections.heading: Referral Disclosure
body_sections.body_html_or_markdown:
Referral Disclosure

Last updated: [Effective Date]

This page explains, in plain language, exactly what Omaha Concrete Lift is, how we make money, and what that means for you as a homeowner.

We Are Not a Contractor

Omaha Concrete Lift is a marketing and referral website. We do not perform concrete leveling, mudjacking, polyjacking, or any related construction or repair work. We are not licensed as a contractor, and nothing on this Site should be interpreted as a claim that we are a licensed contractor or that we perform physical work on your property.

How We Make Money

When you submit a quote request through our contact form, we forward your project details to one or more independent, local concrete leveling contractors. Those contractors may pay Omaha Concrete Lift a referral fee, lead fee, or similar form of compensation for that introduction. This is our primary business model. It costs you nothing, and it should not change the price a contractor quotes you for the work.

We Do Not Guarantee the Lowest Price

We do not negotiate pricing on your behalf, and we do not guarantee that any contractor we connect you with offers the lowest available price for your project. We encourage you to request multiple quotes and compare them before making a decision.

We Do Not Endorse or Warrant Any Specific Contractor

Being included in our referral network is not an endorsement, certification, or guarantee of any contractor's licensing status, insurance coverage, workmanship, reliability, or business practices. We do not independently verify every credential of every contractor in our network on an ongoing basis, and we make no warranty, express or implied, about the outcome of any work performed by a contractor you are matched with.

We Do Not Display Our Own Reviews or Ratings

Because Omaha Concrete Lift does not perform concrete leveling work, we do not have customer reviews of our own workmanship to display, and we do not publish invented or third-party reviews as if they were ours. Any reviews of contractor work belong to the contractor, not to us.

Verify Before You Hire

Before agreeing to any work or payment, we strongly encourage you to:

  • Ask the contractor directly for proof of their business license and liability insurance.
  • Independently verify licensing status through the appropriate state or local licensing authority, if applicable in your jurisdiction.
  • Get a written estimate, scope of work, and any warranty terms in writing before work begins.
  • Confirm payment terms directly with the contractor — Omaha Concrete Lift is not involved in, and does not process, payment for contractor work.

Your Consent to Be Contacted

By submitting a quote request, you consent to being contacted by Omaha Concrete Lift and/or the contractor(s) your request is shared with, by phone, text/SMS, or email, regarding your project, as described in our Privacy Policy and on our contact page.

Questions

If you have questions about how our referral model works, contact us at [Business Contact Email].

mainEntity.name: Why does concrete sink or settle in the first place?

acceptedAnswer.text: Concrete slabs themselves don't usually deteriorate — the soil underneath them does. Common causes include soil compaction over time, erosion from water runoff, poor original sub-base preparation, freeze-thaw cycles, and organic material that decomposes under the slab and leaves a void. Once support underneath the slab is lost, gravity and traffic load cause it to settle unevenly.

mainEntity.name: What's the difference between mudjacking and polyjacking?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mudjacking uses a cement-based slurry pumped beneath the slab to fill voids and lift it, typically through larger drilled holes. Polyjacking uses an expanding polyurethane foam injected through smaller holes. Foam is generally lighter and more water-resistant, while slurry is a heavier, longer-established material. Cost, hole size, cure time, and suitability for your specific project varies by contractor and by soil/site conditions — a local contractor can advise which fits your project best.

mainEntity.name: How much does concrete leveling cost?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cost varies by contractor, region, slab size, method (mudjacking vs. polyjacking), and how much lifting is needed. There isn't a single reliable number we can quote here — pricing varies by contractor and project, which is exactly why getting a few quotes from local pros is useful.

mainEntity.name: How long does a concrete leveling job typically take?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many residential leveling jobs (a driveway panel, a sidewalk slab, a small patio) can be completed in a matter of hours to a single day, but this varies by contractor, method, equipment, and the size/scope of the project. A contractor can give you a project-specific estimate after assessing the site.

mainEntity.name: Is concrete leveling a permanent fix?

acceptedAnswer.text: Concrete leveling addresses the existing void and settling at the time of the repair, but if the underlying cause (drainage, soil erosion, an ongoing leak, etc.) isn't resolved, settling can recur over time. Ask your contractor what, if anything, they recommend to address the root cause, and what warranty (if any) they offer — warranty terms vary by contractor.

mainEntity.name: Can concrete leveling fix a cracked slab, or do I need full replacement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Leveling raises a slab back toward its original position; it doesn't repair existing cracks, though many contractors can seal or patch cracks as part of the job. Whether leveling makes sense versus full replacement depends on the extent of cracking, slab age, and condition — this varies by contractor and by inspection findings.

mainEntity.name: Is concrete leveling less expensive than replacing the slab?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, leveling costs less than full slab removal and replacement, since it reuses the existing concrete rather than requiring demolition, disposal, forming, and a new pour. That said, actual cost comparisons vary by contractor, project scope, and site conditions — a quote from a local pro is the most reliable way to compare.

mainEntity.name: Will concrete leveling affect my landscaping or driveway access?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most leveling methods involve small drilled holes and don't require large-scale excavation, so impact on landscaping is typically minimal compared to full replacement. Access needs (e.g., temporarily blocking a driveway) vary by contractor and project — ask about this when you get your quote.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to be home when the contractor comes out?

acceptedAnswer.text: This depends on the contractor's process and whether it's an initial assessment or the actual leveling work. Many contractors can provide an initial estimate without you being present, but policies vary — the contractor who contacts you can confirm what's needed.

mainEntity.name: How do I verify a contractor is licensed and insured?

acceptedAnswer.text: Always ask any contractor directly for proof of their business license, insurance, and any relevant certifications before hiring them, and verify this information independently if possible (for example, through Nebraska or Iowa state licensing resources, if applicable in your area). Omaha Concrete Lift does not verify, certify, or guarantee the licensing or insurance status of contractors in its network — see our referral disclosure page.
